Part 01

The agent now: the flow and the stack

After Tier 1. What changed, the path a message takes through the real products, three messages step by step, the stack, and where it sits in the goal.

Support agent · after Tier 1 · 18 September 2026

The agent now: the flow and the stack

Between 13 and 18 September the agent stopped running on stand-ins. It now signs customers in through Keycloak, answers from a real store, waits for people on Temporal, and every turn is a trace in Langfuse. This part is what it looks like today; the parts after it were written before, and each says so.

1,149tests passing
38 / 38scenarios pass against the simulated shop
29 / 33say the same against real Saleor (shadow mode)
0.98live pass rate with the real model (T-050)
5real products behind it, each in its own Docker profile

What changed, in one table

Every row replaced something the agent used to do for itself. That is the goal's rule — adopt open source, build only the delta — applied one concern at a time.

ConcernBefore (13 Sep)NowItem

The modelGroq, called directlyLiteLLM proxy with the agent's own key, a rate limit and a budget; the provider is checked at startupT-029, T-018
Waiting for a personA row the agent wrote, polled on the customer's next message; a sweeper loop lapsed escalationsTemporal workflows. The agent can ask and read, never grant; a granted refund is issued the moment it is granted; lapses are timersT-028

Three messages, step by step

A question it answers alone

“where is AB-10001?”
  1. Keycloak's token is verified; the customer id comes from it, never from the text.
  2. The router sees an order-status question and takes the direct route: no model call.
  3. One read, get_order, to the store server, which checks the token and that AB-10001 is this customer's.
  4. Saleor answers fulfilled; the server says shipped — Saleor records dispatch, not arrival.
  5. “Order AB-10001 is currently shipped.” Cost: one read, no tokens.

An action it confirms first

“I don't need AB-10002 anymore” · “yes”
  1. The model proposes cancel_order. The customer never said cancel, so the policy refuses the call and the agent asks.
  2. The customer says “yes”: that turns the pending question into consent for exactly this order.
  3. The call runs, with an idempotency key the store remembers.
  4. The store checks the order is still pending, and cancels it in Saleor.
  5. The reply says cancelled only because the store's result says so.

A refund that needs a person

“refund AB-10003 please”
  1. The agent asks Temporal for an approval. The workflow reads the order's total itself, and it is over the limit.
  2. The customer is told a colleague will authorise it, and that nothing is refunded yet.
  3. A colleague grants it, or the 24-hour timer expires. The customer can leave; the wait survives restarts.
  4. On a grant, the workflow's worker — its own Keycloak login, no refund scope of its own — calls the store, naming the approval. The store checks the approval, then grants the refund against the order's payment.
  5. Next time the customer writes, the agent reads the approval and says what became of it.

Temporal, LangGraph, a queue, or just Postgres

All four can take part in "wait for a person, then do something". They differ in what they do on their own, and so in what you would have to write yourself. The rows are what the refund approval and the escalation actually need.

What the wait needsPostgres tableA job queue (Celery, pg-boss)LangGraph interruptTemporal
Remember that something is waitingyes, a rowa pending jobyes, a checkpointyes, a workflow
Survive the process restartingyesyes, if the broker is durableyes, with a durable checkpointeryes — tested by restarting the container
Fire a deadline with nobody polling (expire at 24 h, lapse at 30 min)no — someone must checka delayed job, cancelled by hand if decided firstno — it waits to be resumedyes, a timer in the workflow
Act the moment the decision arrives, not when the customer next writesnoif the decider enqueues a jobif the decider resumes the graphyes, an update wakes the workflow
Retry the side effect after a crash, exactly where it stoppednoretries the whole jobre-runs the nodeyes, the activity is retried, the steps before it are not
One owner of the state, with rules checked on every changeanyone who can write the rowno state, only jobsthe graph, but the caller supplies the resume valueyes — the update's validator is our rule
A queue a colleague can seea querythe broker's own viewbuild ita queue workflow (and Temporal's UI)
Act under a separate login from the agentbuild ita separate workerit is the agent's processa separate worker
Extra infrastructurenonea broker (or none, with pg-boss)none beyond the checkpointera server (~100 MB here)
Postgres

Remembers that something is waiting. Everything that should happen — the expiry, the refund when granted, the retry — is code you write, schedule and keep correct.

A job queue

Runs work later, with retries. It does not know an approval exists between jobs, so "who decided, and is it still valid" lives somewhere else.

LangGraph interrupt

Pauses the agent's graph and resumes it later with a human's answer. Natural inside LangGraph; it has no timers and acts in the agent's own process.

Temporal

Runs the wait itself: it holds the state, fires the deadline, wakes on the decision, retries the effect, in a process of its own. We keep only the rules. The cost is one more server to run.

That is why the Open Stack uses Temporal and keeps conversations in Postgres. The LangGraph cycle (T-036) will test whether an interrupt can do the same job there; Postgres-native engines (DBOS, Hatchet) are the lighter option worth evaluating.

Scenario 2 — "Connect me to a human"

Yes, this uses Temporal: every escalation is an EscalationWorkflow. Run live on 18 September against the app on Saleor; the replies below are the real ones, and every turn is a trace in Langfuse.

The purple bar is the workflow's life: from the customer's request to the colleague's close. Nothing polls it; Temporal holds it and its timer.

What each piece did

StepWhoWhat happened
1Agent · routerRecognised a request for a person (rule asked-for-human). Deterministic: no model call, no cost.
2Agent → TemporalStarted EscalationWorkflow with the reason, the rule, and a hand-off built from the conversation's facts, so the colleague need not ask again. The record exists before the customer is told anything.
3AgentTold the customer the reference, and a wait estimated from the desk's capacity — not a promise it cannot back.
4AgentOn the next message, asked the workflow: still queued, so it did not answer over the colleague.
5Colleague · /opsSaw it in the queue (the reviewer's own Keycloak login, read-only scope) and closed it with an outcome. The workflow's validator refused nothing here; it would have refused the customer closing their own case, a second close, or a close after the lapse.
6AgentNext message: the workflow says resolved, so the conversation is the agent's again.
—TemporalHeld the escalation, would have lapsed it at 30 minutes, and kept it across restarts. Our code decided what escalation means: the rule, the wording, the outcome labels, who may close.

Try it yourself

  1. In the chat, type Connect me to a human. Note the E- reference.
  2. Type anything else: it is held — still with a colleague.
  3. As the colleague: GET /ops/escalations with the reviewer token the app printed, then POST /ops/escalations/E-…/resolve with {"outcome": "resolved"}.
  4. Ask about an order again: the agent answers.

MCP, explained like you're five

The picture

The agent is someone who cannot cook. The store is a kitchen. MCP is the menu and the order ticket that every waiter and every kitchen agree on, so any agent can order from any kitchen without learning its language first.

What happens
  1. Read the menu — tools/list. The kitchen says what it can make and what each dish needs.
  2. Write a ticket — tools/call with a dish and its details, e.g. cancel_order {id: AB-10002}.
  3. Clip your ID to the ticket — _meta. The kitchen checks it itself and ignores what you say you are.
  4. Get the plate and a receipt — the result, as text and as structured data the agent can check.

Two kinds of “no”, and MCP keeps them apart: the kitchen tried and could not (an execution error — “that order has shipped”), or the ticket never reached a kitchen that understood it (a protocol error — no such dish). The agent treats them differently: the first it can explain to the customer, the second is a fault.

One tool call, on the wire

The model chooses which tool and writes its arguments. Everything that decides whether it is allowed — the token, the approval, the idempotency key — travels in _meta, which the model never sees or writes.

Today, and after T-054

The code already behaves as if the two were apart: the store verifies a token addressed to itself and trusts nothing the caller asserts. T-054 makes the process boundary real.

How it follows the MCP standard

The specificationWhat we doStatus
JSON-RPC 2.0, an initialize handshake agreeing capabilitiesthe official SDK does both, on each sidefollows
tools/list: name, description, inputSchema (JSON Schema)six tools, schemas generated from the Python signaturesfollows
outputSchema and structuredContent (optional)required by our client: a tool without one is refused, so results are compared, not parsedstricter
tools/call; a failed tool returns isError: true, a bad request is a JSON-RPC errorboth kept apart as execution and protocol errorsfollows
_meta for extension data, keys with a prefixrequest keys are aoas/session, aoas/approval, aoas/idempotency-key; the tool-level side_effect and required_scope have no prefixmostly · T-054
Tool annotations: readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHintnot set; our side_effect says the same and more (reversible vs irreversible), but only our client reads itmissing · T-054
Transports: stdio, or streamable HTTPthe SDK's in-memory transport, in one processnot yet · T-054
Authorization: OAuth 2.1 on the HTTP connectionno connection auth (no HTTP); the customer's exchanged token rides per call in _meta, because one connection serves many customers and the store must know whose each call isT-054: both
Resources, prompts, sampling, rootsnot used: the agent needs tools, nothing elsenot needed
Elicitation (the server asks the user a question mid-call)considered for approvals and rejected: the approver is not the caller, and an approval can take a day — a Temporal workflow insteadchosen not to

Are we using FastMCP?

Yes — the one in the official SDK

FastMCP 1.0 was merged into the official MCP Python SDK, and in SDK 2.x (we run mcp 2.1.1) it was renamed MCPServer. That is what order_system/server.py and AgentTwin's projection build on: the @server.tool decorator, schemas from type hints, Context for _meta. Importing mcp.server.fastmcp in this SDK raises an error pointing at the rename.

No — the separate fastmcp package

The standalone FastMCP 2.x project adds server composition, proxies, servers generated from OpenAPI, auth providers and a richer client. We need none of that yet: one server, six hand-written tools, one client. The official SDK is one dependency, versioned with the specification, and our import contract keeps MCP inside one module, so moving later is a small change. Worth another look at T-054 if its auth helpers save writing the connection's OAuth.

Knowing first: watching the agent in production

The question: if the agent stops doing its job in production, does the person running it find out before a customer does? On 18 September the answer was no — every trace was in Langfuse and nothing told anyone. On 19 September it is yes: the numbers leave the process to Prometheus, 21 alert rules decide what pages, a synthetic customer crosses every hop every ten minutes, and 22 rules read sampled turns and write their verdicts back as Langfuse scores. This section is what an operator asks, what answers it, and the rule catalog behind it.

Three kinds of eval, and what each needs

EvalWhen it runsWhat it needsHere
Offlinebefore a release, on fixed cases (AAC stages S1–S3)a world that answers the same way every time, and recorded model answershave AgentTwin scenarios, golden files, cassettes, baseline.json, shadow mode against Saleor
Inlineinside the request, before the reply goes out (S4)checks fast and certain enough to block onhalf policy, schemas, the store's own refusals, the unbacked-promise check. The inline grader (AHC-0028) is not built — G0.11
Onlineafter the fact, on production (S5), and on a schedule (S6)what was said, what the tools returned, what happened afterwards, somewhere to write scores, and rates somebody alerts onhave watch/ over Langfuse, scores back to Langfuse, rates to Prometheus; the canary on a schedule (S6). Left: a model-graded rubric, once it is checked against labels (AAC-0084)

Is what we send to OpenTelemetry enough?

What is sent

35 span types, each held to a contract (telemetry/contract.py): the route and why, each tool with its side effect and idempotency key, the escalation rule and outcome, approvals, tokens, model, cost per call and per run, why a run ended, context size, unbacked promises, breaker and retries, and user.id / session.id on the root so Langfuse groups by conversation.

And seven counters with bounded labels (telemetry/counters.py): turns, escalations, refusals, approvals, unbacked promises, spend, model calls.

What looking found, and what closed it
  1. The counters went nowhere. No MeterProvider was configured, so all seven recorded into a no-op. T-055
  2. Approvals counted only requested; an expiry happens on a timer nobody watches, so the workflow counts it itself now, through Temporal's meter. T-055
  3. No latency anywhere: turn, model call and each tool are histograms now, the model's under the conventions' own name. T-055
  4. No words were ever captured. set_payload was off by default and called from nowhere, so switching it on captured nothing. T-057
  5. Tool arguments and results were not on the tool span. T-057
  6. Nothing wrote a score back, and nothing joined what happened later to the run. T-057
  7. Spend was recorded per model call as a running total, so one run landed in the histogram once per call, at a different size each time. T-055
  8. The trace still stops at the MCP hop. T-020

Six of the eight were invisible from the code: each was written, reviewed, and reached nothing. That is the argument for a test that reads the numbers back.

The record online eval needs: AHC-0114, field by field

AHC-0114 names the minimum a unit of work must leave so it can be judged later without re-running it: nine groups, each answering one question. Structure is recorded for every turn; the words, for a declared sample, redacted.

GroupAnswersWhat it holdsHere
1 · Join keyswhose, and which turn?run id, session, pseudonymous user, tenant, position in the sessionhave agent.run.id, session.id, user.id, agent.tenant
2 · Versionswhich release?config fingerprint, model asked for and model that answered, each rule set's versionhave fingerprint, gen_ai.request/response.model, router, escalation and promise rule versions
3 · Inputwhat was asked?the customer's message, redacted — sampledhave for a sampled turn, redacted
4 · What it was shownwhat did it know?each tool result, redacted, with its source — sampledhave each result as JSON, for a sampled turn
5 · What it didwhat path?model calls; tool calls with arguments, side effect and outcome; policy decisionshave and the arguments, on a sampled turn
6 · Output and endingwhat came out, and how did it end?the reply, redacted — sampled; completed · refused · escalated · waiting · failed, and the rulehave the ending, the rule, and the reply on a sampled turn
7 · Cost and timewhat did it cost?tokens, cost, duration, per turn and per callhave on spans and as metrics
8 · Markerswhat kind of run?synthetic or real, content captured or not, resolution modehave synthetic, captured and resolution
9 · Later outcomeswas it right?kind, source and time of what happened afterwardsfour of five the escalation verdict, returned, asked for a person, feedback. A reversal has no source in this store

Structure on every turn; the words on a declared sample (AGENT_CAPTURE_SAMPLE), redacted before they leave the process, and the sample marked so no rate is computed over it by accident.

Why Prometheus and Grafana beside OpenTelemetry and Langfuse

OpenTelemetry is a format and a way to ship data, not a place to keep it. A trace is everything about one request — large, often sampled, slow to count across thousands. A metric is a number already counted — tiny, kept for months, and checked against alert rules every few seconds. Langfuse is built to read and score traces; Prometheus is built to hold numbers and alert on them; Grafana puts every source on one screen, including Temporal, Postgres and Keycloak, which already publish Prometheus metrics. An exemplar joins the two: a spike on a chart links to one trace that was in it.

None of the right-hand side is in compose.yaml yet. T-055 adds the Collector, Prometheus, Grafana and Alertmanager.

Catching it automatically: six levels

An agent that has stopped doing its job usually still answers every request with a 200. So the levels that matter most are the ones above “is it up”.

LevelWhat it catchesHowTells someone by
L0 · Upa dependency down: Temporal, Keycloak, Saleor, LiteLLM, the providerhealth checks, the breaker's statepage
L1 · Speed and errorsslow or failing turns, model calls, toolslatency and error metrics against an SLO, alert on burn ratepage
L2 · Behaviour rates ★working and wrong: escalations from 8% to 30% after a release, one rule refusing everything, the step limit hit, junk from the model, approvals expiring, p95 cost doublingthe seven counters, exported, against last week's baseline — AAC-0114page on a sharp shift, Slack on a drift
L3 · Canary ★broken while nobody is using it: a rotated key, an expired secret, a store changeeight scenarios every ten minutes through the deployed edge, as a test customer in a namespace only it owns — AAC-0116page
L4 · Online qualityworse answers: a reply that contradicts its tool's result, the wrong policy, tonescore a sample: certain checks first, a validated judge second, and later outcomes — came back within a day, asked for a person, refund reversed — AAC-0014, AAC-0115a trend to Slack, never a page: a judge is noisy
L5 · Release drifta release behaves differentlyL2 and L4 by config fingerprint, rolled out behind a flag (T-047)stop the rollout

★ First: cheap, certain, and between them they catch most “the agent stopped doing its job” before a customer does. L4 then says whether it is doing it well, slowly.

pass^kthe chance a scenario passes on every one of k runs — the reliability number (τ-bench)T-007

Elsewherepromptfoo (T-046), DeepEval and Inspect (T-040), Ragas, Braintrust, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix for evals; NeMo Guardrails, Guardrails AI, Llama Guard for guardrails; Toxiproxy for faults; k6 and Locust for load; LiteLLM budgets, fallbacks and rate limits at the gateway

The rule catalog: 22 rules over turns, 21 over rates

A cost analyser has a few hundred rules for Spark anti-patterns; this is the same idea over an agent's telemetry. The catalog of what can go wrong lives in the assurance catalog as patterns (AACP-xxxx) — 56 of them, each with a symptom, a mechanism, the obligations that catch it, and now a signal: the fields a monitor reads, the rule, a starting threshold and how loudly to say so. A rule here implements one pattern's signal, and carries its id.

Two engines, because there are two questions

Per turn and per conversation — did this answer contradict its own lookup? — is our code, because only we know what get_order returning pending means. It runs over sampled turns read back from Langfuse and writes a score per finding.

Per window — is this rate twice last week's? — is Prometheus, whose rule language and alert routing are older and better than anything we would write. Thresholds live in a file an operator can read and change without a deploy.

Severity is what happens next

page: certain, and a customer is being misled right now — a reply that contradicts the store, a claimed action that did not happen, personal data in a reply, a write after injected instructions, the canary failing.

ticket: read this week. trend: only ever a rate, so it is a recording rule and a panel, never a page. A trend that pages is a trend nobody reads twice.

A rule that needs the words does not run on a turn whose words were not sampled, and that turn is not counted as passing it: a contradiction nobody could see is not an absence of contradictions.

Ten patterns with a signal and no detector

Stated rather than quietly missing, in watch/rules.py's NOT_YET, each with what is in the way. One is left: turns to resolution (AACP-0043), because nothing marks a conversation resolved — the watch infers when an answer did not hold, never that one did. The other nine of T-058 are detected: the configuration fingerprint on the rates and tokens (0002, 0055), truncations, unoffered tools and schema failures counted apart (0004, 0023, 0024), tools offered as a metric (0026), the desk's verdict by rule (0044), tokens per turn in the record (0003) and one form for model names (0054). A test fails if a pattern is both detected and owed.

Found by running it

What ranWhat it found
The canary, against the live stack — Keycloak, LiteLLM, the model, the store's MCP server, Saleor4/4 pass. On the way: F-048 — the model writes order ids with a non-breaking hyphen, CN‑70002, so a check for CN-70002 fails on a right answer and a customer pasting it into a search finds nothing. Every rule now reads replies with dashes normalised; the agent still shows the customer what the model wrote.
The canary, against the simulated shopF-047 — asking for another customer's order is a tool error there and found: false in Saleor, so the agent answers a 502 where it should answer plainly. Two stores disagreeing about what not yours means.
The watch, over the first live turnsThree batches of spans timed out on the way to Langfuse and two of seven turns were never evaluated. Traces now go through the collector's queue and retries, and its own counters raise TelemetryDropping — a new pattern, AACP-0056.
The outcome rules, over that trafficEight returned outcomes on one answer, because a customer asking four questions in a minute looked like four failures. Version 2 of the inference ignores anything within 30 minutes; version 3 counts a burst once.
Rules against real replies“AB-10002 cannot be cancelled” read as the order is cancelled. A status now counts only where it is asserted — is, was, has been — and not where it is negated.

Five corrections in one evening's use, four of them things no test would have said. That is the argument for a canary: it uses the system the way a customer does, on a schedule.

Did the specs say any of this?

Partly. AAC already had the right stages — S5 online eval, S6 scheduled regression — and AAC-0014 (score sampled traffic), AAC-0016 (re-run frozen cases), AAC-0007 (latency) and AAC-0008 (cost per task). What nothing required was the part this section is about: noticing that the system has stopped working. So, spec first, these went in on 19 September:

All six are exercised by tests now, and `patterns/` gained a signal block plus 38 patterns (AACP-0019 to 0056) — the catalog the rules above implement. One question is left open: AAC-0084 (validate a judge against human labels) applies only to A10, and an A6 agent scored by a judge online needs it too, which is why the judge is the last piece and not the first.

Agent harness tutorial

What an agent harness is, what goes in one, and how to build it, one question at a time — from the kinds of AI application down to this agent's function stack.

Tutorial

Agent Harness Tutorial

What an agent harness is, what goes in one, and how to build it, one question at a time.

Questions

  1. 01What are the different kinds and shapes of AI application?
  2. 02What layers make up a whole AI application?
  3. 03What does an agent harness have to take care of?
  4. 04What does the support reference agent look like, end to end?

Question 01

What are the different kinds and shapes of AI application?

AI applications come in ten shapes. The industry you're in, which model you use and how big it is don't set the shape. Two questions do:

  1. Who owns control flow? Your code, or the model?
  2. What does the output touch? A person reading it, code consuming it, or the real world?

The shape matters because it decides what the harness around the model has to do. Each shape adds a new way to fail, so each one needs more from the harness.

#ShapeWhat it isControl flowExamples
A1Single-Turn Transform One call in, one answer out. No tools, no retrieval, no memory. The model reworks the text it was given. Your codeClassify, summarise, translate, rewrite
A2Structured Extractor Output is a typed object read by downstream code, not by a person. A schema turns quality failures into type failures. Your codeEntity extraction, form filling, function arguments
A3Grounded Answerer Search a set of documents, then write an answer from what came back. The search step and the writing step fail independently, so each is tested on its own. Your codeRAG, document Q&A, knowledge assistant
A4Conversational Assistant Multi-turn and stateful. Keeps context, memory and user history across turns, but takes no action on its own. Your codeSupport chat, tutoring, guided intake
A5Deterministic Workflow A fixed graph of steps with an LLM call at each node. The handoffs between steps are where new failures appear. Your codeChains, pipelines, batch enrichment
A6Tool-Using Agent The model picks which tools to call, in what order, and when to stop. This is the biggest jump in what you have to test. The modelReAct loops, function-calling agents
A7Multi-Agent System Several agents hand work to each other, under a supervisor or by passing it along. On top of A6, it adds failures in who is allowed to do what, how much each may spend, and how far one agent's mistake can spread. Several modelsSupervisor/worker, specialist handoff
A8Artifact Producer Output is code, SQL, config or a document that will be run or shipped. You can check it by running it, which is the strongest check any shape gets. EitherCode generation, text-to-SQL, infrastructure-as-code
A9Autonomous Operator Runs unattended on a trigger or schedule, with real side effects and nobody watching live. The model, unattendedScheduled agents, auto-remediation, background workers
A10Classifier · Router · Judge The model's output steers other machinery: a routing decision, a guardrail verdict, a quality score. You won't see its errors unless you evaluate the evaluator. Your codeLLM-as-judge, safety classifiers, model routers

Shapes are tags, not a tree

A real system usually has more than one shape. A support agent like the one in this repo is a Conversational Assistant (A4), a Tool-Using Agent (A6) and a Grounded Answerer (A3) all at once. It may also use a Router (A10) to decide when to hand off to a human. Give a system every shape that applies and build the harness for all of them.

Why this matters for the harness

Every shape needs a common core from the harness: input handling, output checks, tracing, cost limits, evaluation. Beyond that core, each shape adds what is new about it. The line that matters most runs between A5 and A6. Up to A5, your code decides what happens next. From A6 on, the model decides, so the harness has to supply the limits your code used to enforce: which tools are allowed, step and cost budgets, stop conditions, and approval before irreversible actions.

In the AI Harness Catalog (AHC), a single-turn transform (A1) needs about 50 harness capabilities, while a multi-agent system (A7) needs about 75. The more control the model has, the more the harness has to do.

Question 02

What layers make up a whole AI application?

A request travels left to right: from the person, through your application and your harness, optionally through an AI gateway, to the model provider that runs the model. The answer comes back the same way. Underneath, a lab trained the model and a cloud runs every box. Each box is a role. One company can fill several roles, which is where most of the confusion comes from.

LayerWhat it doesExamplesYou…
1 · ApplicationWhere a person, or a trigger, starts the work and sees the result.Chat UI, IDE, Slack bot, API, schedulerBuild
2 · Orchestration & contextDecides the steps, assembles what the model sees, retrieves documents, keeps memory, and calls tools.Claude Agent SDK, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, plain code, MCP servers, pgvectorBuild
3 · AI gateway (optional)A proxy in front of the providers. It gives all your apps one API and enforces keys, budgets, rate limits, routing and fallback. It runs no model itself.LiteLLM Proxy, Portkey, Kong AI Gateway, Azure APIM, Databricks AI GatewayRun, or buy as a service
4 · Model providerRuns the model on its GPUs and serves it through an API. You pay per token.Anthropic API, OpenAI API, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, Azure AI Foundry, Databricks Model Serving, self-hosted vLLMRent
5 · ModelThe trained weights: the LLM, plus embedding models for search.Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, Voyage embeddingsChoose (a config value)
LabTrains the model. Not in the request path.Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta, MistralNothing
Cloud & computeThe machines under every box: yours and the provider's.AWS, Azure, GCP, Databricks, NVIDIA GPUsRent
Across your sideKeeps your side of the line safe, measured and affordable.Guardrails, eval suites, tracing, budgets, permissions, human approvalBuild

Four pairs people confuse

PairThe difference
Gateway vs providerA gateway forwards requests. A provider runs the model. LiteLLM or Portkey on its own can't answer a single prompt; it needs a provider behind it. If you remove the gateway, your harness calls the provider directly. That's fine for one app and one provider. Add a gateway when several apps, teams or providers need one set of keys, budgets and logs.
Provider vs labA lab trains the model. A provider serves it. Anthropic is both: the lab that trains Claude and the provider behind the Anthropic API. AWS trains no Claude model, yet Bedrock serves Claude. Meta trains Llama but serves it to almost nobody; you get Llama from Bedrock, Databricks or your own vLLM.
Provider vs cloudAWS the cloud rents you machines (EC2, GPUs). AWS Bedrock is a model provider that happens to run on that cloud. Same company, different layers. Choosing AWS as your cloud doesn't force Bedrock. Your app on AWS can still call the Anthropic API.
Model vs providerOne model, many front doors. The same Claude model is served by the Anthropic API, Bedrock, Vertex and Azure AI Foundry. Features, prices and release timing can differ slightly between them. The model is what thinks; the provider is where you call it.

One company, several roles

CompanyLabModelProviderGatewayCloudHarness tooling
Anthropic✓ClaudeAnthropic API––Claude Agent SDK, MCP
OpenAI✓GPTOpenAI API––Agents SDK
Google✓ DeepMindGeminiVertex AI, Gemini APIApigeeGCPADK
Amazon✓NovaBedrock–AWSBedrock AgentCore
Microsoft✓PhiAzure AI FoundryAzure APIMAzureSemantic Kernel
Meta✓Llama (open weights)––––
Databricks✓DBRX (older)Model ServingAI Gatewayruns on AWS/Azure/GCPMosaic AI Agent Framework
LiteLLM · Portkey · Kong–––✓––

So when someone says "we use Anthropic", ask which role they mean. It could be the model (Claude), the provider (the Anthropic API) or the framework (the Agent SDK). Each is a separate choice.

How one request flows

  1. A person, or a trigger, sends a request through the application.
  2. The harness (orchestration & context) builds the prompt. It pulls relevant documents through RAG, recalls memory, and lists the tools the model may use.
  3. If there is a gateway, it checks the key and budget, logs the call, and picks a provider.
  4. The provider runs the model, which either answers or asks for a tool. If it asks for a tool, the harness runs the tool, feeds the result back, and loops to step 3.
  5. The answer passes back through output guardrails to the person. Tracing and cost records are written along the way.

Where the harness sits

The model is one box on the far right, and you rent it. Most of the engineering, and every failure from Question 01, lives in the outlined parts: orchestration & context and the cross-cutting band. That is the agent harness, everything around the model that makes it safe and dependable to run. The gateway is drawn dashed because it's optional. When you have one, it enforces some of the harness's controls, such as budgets and key management, at a single shared point.

Question 03

What does an agent harness have to take care of?

The harness is everything that is neither the model nor your business logic: the ordinary, predictable code that turns a model into a system. The AI Harness Catalog (AHC) splits it into 16 areas. Each one owns a single question, such as "what is the model told?" or "when does the system stop?"

Most teams build two of them, observability and evals, and call the harness done. The other fourteen are where agents fail in production.

Five groups make the sixteen easier to remember:

#Area · the question it ownsWhat it coversWhat breaks without it
What goes in and out of the model
L1Context assembly
What is the model told?		 Prompt templates and versions, where retrieved text goes, ordering, compaction, token budget, fencing untrusted content.AHC-0011 · Untrusted content is fenced and labelled at assembly Text inside a support ticket is read as an instruction. The budget silently truncates the evidence the answer needed.
L2Model invocation
How is the call made?		 One client, explicit parameters, streaming, timeouts, which models can be reached, processing region.AHC-0004 · One choke point for every model call Calls are scattered, so there is no single place to add limits, logging or a new provider. Parameters change when the SDK default changes.
L6I/O contracts
What can the caller rely on?		 Input validation, typed parsing of every response, a typed outcome that includes "failed" and "abstained".AHC-0001 · Every model response crosses a typed boundary A malformed response surfaces as a KeyError three layers away. The caller can't tell "no answer" from "error".
What the agent can do, remember, and when it stops
L3Tool layer
What can the model do?		 Tool schemas, argument validation before dispatch, sandboxing, size limits on results, reversibility class, authority checked where the tool runs.AHC-0039 · Tools are classified by reversibility, and the class gates dispatch The model invents arguments. A 2 MB tool result floods the context. A delete runs as easily as a read.
L4Control loop
When does the system stop?		 Iteration, step and budget accounting, stop conditions, no-progress detection, bounds on delegation depth and fan-out.AHC-0042 · The loop has a no-progress condition, not only a step ceiling The agent calls the same tool forever. Sub-agents delegate in a cycle. Cost climbs until someone notices.
L5State & memory
What is remembered?		 Conversation state, checkpoints, history compaction, long-term memory, isolation between sessions and tenants, what survives a crash.AHC-0069 · Memory writes go through a gate, not straight from the model A crash loses half-done work. One customer's memory leaks into another's session. The model saves a false "fact" that persists.
Keeping it safe
L7Policy enforcement
Where does a rule become real?		 Guardrail checks on input and output, closed by default, redaction before data leaves, policies applied in a declared order, every decision recorded.AHC-0008 · One enforcement position, defaulting closed The guardrail exists in a design doc but no code path enforces it. Personal data is sent to the provider.
L16Identity & authorization
Who is the system acting as?		 The end user's identity carried to every tool, authorization of each action, secrets kept out of prompts, entitlement filtering in retrieval.AHC-0034 · The end user's identity reaches every downstream decision The agent acts with an admin service account for every user. An API key ends up in a prompt. RAG shows documents the user may not see.
L14Human-in-the-loop
Where can a person step in?		 Approval gates, escalation that carries context, a stop button outside the run, what the system does while it waits.AHC-0057 · Irreversible actions require an approval the run cannot grant A refund or delete goes through with nobody approving. A human gets the escalation with none of the context.
Keeping it running and affordable
L8Concurrency & flow control
What happens under load?		 Bounded parallelism and fan-out, queueing, backpressure, throttling (429) handled separately from failure, deadlines passed down.AHC-0021 · Throttling is handled as a distinct condition from failure A burst of traffic trips rate limits. Retries turn a slowdown into an outage. Work runs past the caller's deadline.
L10Failure handling
What happens when something breaks?		 Bounded retries, fallback, idempotency, compensating actions, typed partial results, a declared degradation path.AHC-0074 · Every step declares whether repeating it is safe A provider outage becomes your outage. A retry charges a customer twice. A truncated answer is shown as complete.
L13Cost accounting
What does it cost, and who pays?		 Spend tracked per unit of work, attribution tags, a declared price table, ceilings that can stop work already in flight.AHC-0030 · A ceiling exists that can stop work already in flight The bill is the first you hear of it. One runaway run burns the month's budget, and nobody can say which feature spent it.
Knowing what happened, and changing it safely
L11Observability
Can a past run be explained?		 A span per call, one trace ID across the whole unit of work, which route served each call, payload capture with redaction.AHC-0026 · One identifier spans the whole unit of work A customer complains and you can't see what the agent saw, decided or did.
L12Eval harness
Can the system be measured at all?		 A task entrypoint an eval can call, datasets, versioned pluggable graders, CI wiring, production traces turned into test cases.AHC-0010 · A task entrypoint an evaluation can drive Every prompt change is a guess. Quality drifts and nobody notices until users do.
L9Determinism & replay
Can yesterday be reproduced?		 Pinned parameters, recorded fixtures, a swappable fake provider, replaying a past run without the network.AHC-0022 · Provider interaction is substitutable without changing the system A bug can't be reproduced. Tests hit the real API, so they're slow, flaky and cost money.
L15Release & configuration
Which version is running?		 Model pins, prompt versions, feature flags, canary, rollback, and one recorded, resolved configuration per run.AHC-0032 · Rollback restores prompt, model and policy together "What changed?" has no answer. A rollback reverts the prompt but leaves the new model.

Not every shape needs all sixteen

Thirteen areas apply to every shape from Question 01. Three appear only as the model gains control:

  • Tool layer (L3): tool-using agents, multi-agent systems and autonomous operators (A6, A7, A9), plus the sandbox for artifact producers (A8).
  • Control loop (L4): from deterministic workflows (A5) upward. A single-turn transform has no loop to stop.
  • Human-in-the-loop (L14): approvals for agents that act (A6, A7, A9), escalation for assistants (A4), rejection for artifact producers (A8).

State & memory (L5) is a similar case. Every shape owes one core rule about how state is saved, and the rest arrive with conversations (A4) and agents.

Where the areas sit in the Question 02 diagram

  • Orchestration & context box: context assembly, tools, control loop, state & memory, I/O contracts, human-in-the-loop.
  • AI gateway, if you have one: it can carry part of model invocation, concurrency, cost accounting and failure handling (fallback) for every app at once.
  • Cross-cutting band: policy enforcement, identity, observability, evals, determinism, release & configuration.
In AHC, layers and concerns are different things. The 16 above are layers: which part of the harness a rule belongs to. Concerns are a separate tag for which quality a rule serves: the nine ISO/IEC 25010 qualities (reliability, security, safety, maintainability…) plus cost. The catalog holds about 110 rules, and each has one layer and one concern.

Question 04

What does the support reference agent look like, end to end?

The reference agent does customer support for a clothing store. In Question 01's terms it is a tool-using agent (A6). It uses no agent framework, because a framework would own the control loop, context assembly and failure handling, which are the layers this tutorial is about. Instead it has one module per harness area from Question 03, and an import contract that fails the build if a module reaches across the architecture.

Mapped to the roles in Question 02

RoleIn the reference agent
ApplicationChatwoot (chat widget and human desk), the login portal, and a built-in /chat page
Harnesssupport_agent: edge, router, loop, context, policy, tools, approvals, escalation, state, identity, telemetry, cost and the rest, one module per area
AI gatewayLiteLLM proxy. It holds the provider credential and gives the agent its own key with a budget, rate limit and model allowlist.
Model providerGroq, through its OpenAI-compatible API
Modelgpt-oss-120b. A config value, checked against the endpoint at startup.
ToolsThe order system's MCP server (src/order_system) in front of a real Saleor store
CloudLocal Docker Compose: Postgres, LiteLLM, Keycloak, Saleor, plus Langfuse, Temporal and Chatwoot behind profiles

Follow one message

  1. Log in and chat. The customer logs in through the portal (Keycloak) and types in the Chatwoot widget. No token ever reaches the browser; the login is kept server-side.
  2. Edge. Chatwoot's webhook arrives. The agent checks the HMAC signature and a timestamp no more than five minutes old, confirms the contact is verified, resumes that customer's stored login, and takes the delivery id so a resent message can't act twice.
  3. Router. On every turn, a deterministic router decides whether the model is needed at all. Direct answers what the spec can answer. Refuse handles requests like "give me a discount". Escalate handles "get me a human". All three cost nothing and never enter the loop. Only Agentic goes on.
  4. Model call. The loop assembles context, with untrusted text fenced and old history trimmed rather than summarised, and runs the pre-model policy check. The llm module, the only one allowed to import a provider SDK, calls the LiteLLM proxy, which forwards to Groq. The reply is parsed into a typed result and checked by post-model policy.
  5. Tool call. If the model asks for a tool, pre-tool policy runs, then the MCP client calls the order system with the customer's exchanged token and an idempotency key. The server verifies the token and, for a refund, the approval, and only then calls Saleor. The result is capped at 8,000 characters, fenced, and fed back to the model.
  6. Stop. The loop ends when the model is done, or when the harness stops it at 12 steps, $0.50, or the same step repeating three times. The reason is always recorded.
  7. Wait for a person when needed. A refund over ₹10,000 returns NeedsApproval. The turn saves a checkpoint, a Temporal workflow waits for up to 24 hours, and a reviewer decides at the desk. An escalation hands the chat to a person in Chatwoot with the facts attached as a private note.
  8. Reply. The answer goes back through Chatwoot. The trace, redacted before export, goes to Langfuse with the task's cost.

The six tools

ToolKindScope needed
get_order, list_ordersReadThe customer's own orders only, filtered by the verified token
cancel_order, change_addressWriteorders:write
open_return_requestWritereturns:write
issue_refundWrite, money leaves the businessrefunds:write, plus a person's approval above ₹10,000
The architecture is enforced, not just documented. Import contracts in pyproject.toml fail the build if any module except llm imports a provider SDK, any module except tools speaks MCP, or the agent imports the order system or its own simulator. The order system checks the agent's authority independently, so the agent can't learn to satisfy the rules instead of being held to them.

Question 05

End-to-end function stack

What actually runs when a customer sends one message? Each scenario below follows one real turn through the reference agent: every function in order, with its file and line, what it receives and returns, and everything that leaves the process. That covers what goes to the model, over MCP, to Saleor, to Postgres, to Temporal and to OpenTelemetry.

How these were captured. Each scenario is one real turn through the full composed stack:
  • Keycloak-shaped JWT at the edge
  • the real router and loop
  • the model through the LiteLLM proxy to Groq (openai/gpt-oss-120b)
  • the order system's MCP server over the real Saleor store
  • Postgres for the checkpoint, and Temporal for the delivery claim
Every function entry and return in src/ was recorded with Python's sys.monitoring, and the wire payloads were tapped where they leave the process. Nothing is reconstructed. The script is agent-harness-tutorial/capture/capture_turn.py; run it again to get a fresh trace.

Scenario 1 · Happy path: "show me my orders"

A signed-in customer (C-1042) opens a new conversation and types show me my orders. The router finds no intent it can answer on its own, so the turn goes to the loop. The model asks for one tool, reads the result, and answers.

2model calls
1tool call
2,477 / 754tokens in / out
$0.00094metered cost

What crossed each boundary

1 · HTTP in: the request and the token behind it 
{
  "method": "POST",
  "path": "/chat",
  "headers": {
    "Authorization": "Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6…UIn0.x.y",
    "Idempotency-Key": "dlv-cf3cc0efdd",
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
  },
  "body": {
    "text": "show me my orders"
  }
}

The token's claims after verification. Only these decide who the customer is; a customer_id in the body would be ignored.

{
  "sub": "login-C-1042",
  "scp": [
    "orders:read",
    "orders:write",
    "returns:write"
  ],
  "iss": "http://local-issuer.test/realms/support",
  "aud": "support-agent",
  "iat": 1789726648,
  "exp": 1789727548,
  "jti": "3234b11e54eb41999ddf55c8b16dab9e",
  "customer_id": "C-1042"
}
2 · Temporal: the delivery claim

TemporalDeliveries.claim starts a workflow whose id is the delivery id, so a second POST with the same Idempotency-Key finds it already running and gets already handled instead of a second run. settle signals it closed after the turn, even if the turn failed.

{
  "claim": {
    "start_workflow": "DeliveryClaim.run",
    "id": "delivery.dlv-cf3cc0efdd",
    "id_reuse_policy": "ALLOW_DUPLICATE_FAILED_ONLY"
  },
  "settle": {
    "signal": "DeliveryClaim.settle",
    "then": "await handle.result()"
  }
}

9 · HTTP out: the response 
{
  "status": 200,
  "body": {
    "conversation_id": "cnv_7516491332ba4274",
    "reply": "Here are the orders associated with your account (newest first):\n\n| Order ID | Status | Total (₹) | Days Since Delivery* | Final Sale | Return Open |\n|----------|--------|-----------|----------------------|------------|-------------| …",
    "outcome": "completed"
  }
}

What to notice

  • One tool, two model calls. The first call picks the tool; the second writes the answer from its result. The second is about 5× larger because the whole order list goes back in.
  • Identity never comes from the model or the body. It is verified at the edge. A new token addressed to the order system travels in MCP _meta, and the order system verifies it again before it touches Saleor.
  • The tool surface depends on the customer. issue_refund is on the server but hidden from this customer, who lacks refunds:write. The model is offered request_refund, a local tool that routes through approvals.
  • Policy ran at five points: pre-model twice, pre-tool, post-tool, post-model, and the final reply screen. The post-model check took the longest (about 30 ms), because it confirms every order id in the reply appears in the tool result.
  • Reads skip the ledger. An idempotency key was minted (run…:0:1) but not sent, because list_orders is a read.
  • Postgres was written once: a single checkpoint row at the end. Nothing was written during the loop.
  • Cached tokens are billed as full input. Groq reported 256 cached prompt tokens on call 1, but _from_wire doesn't read prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens, so the meter prices them at the full input rate. The cost is slightly overstated, never understated.

Scenario 2 · Human escalation: "Connect me to a human"

The same customer opens a new conversation and asks for a person. This is not one turn but a conversation and a colleague: the agent raises an escalation, holds the line while it is open, a colleague closes it from the desk, and the agent takes the conversation back. The wait in the middle is a Temporal workflow, EscalationWorkflow, with a 30-minute timer that lapses it if nobody comes.

Captured the same way as scenario 1, by agent-harness-tutorial/capture/capture_escalation.py: four steps through the real HTTP edge and the desk's routes, every function in src/ recorded, plus the workflow's own history read back from Temporal. The tracer runs inside Temporal's sandbox too, which made two workflow tasks fail and retry during the capture (without it: none), so Temporal's timings below are inflated.

6 · Spans, per trace 
{
  "1 · raise": [
    "http.chat",
    "agent.turn",
    "agent.route",
    "agent.escalation.raise",
    "agent.policy"
  ],
  "2 · held": [
    "http.chat",
    "agent.turn",
    "agent.escalation.wait"
  ],
  "3 · desk": [
    "agent.escalation.queue",
    "agent.escalation.resolve"
  ],
  "4 · handed back": [
    "http.chat",
    "agent.turn",
    "agent.route",
    "agent.direct",
    "agent.tools.list",
    "tools/list",
    "tools/call get_order",
    "agent.tool",
    "agent.policy"
  ]
}

What to notice

  • No model, anywhere. A request for a person is recognised by the router's rule, and the hold in step 2 returns before the router is even consulted. The whole escalation cost no tokens.
  • The record comes before the words. raise_for starts the workflow and reads it back before _handoff_text writes the reply, so the reference the customer is given always exists.
  • The wait is measured, not promised. “About 5 minutes” is the queue's depth (1) at the desk's capacity (12 an hour). With no capacity configured the reply promises a reference and no time.
  • The agent and the colleague never talk. Each reads and writes the workflow: the agent through TemporalEscalations (raise, read), the desk through EscalationDesk (close). Neither handle can do the other's job.
  • Our rules, Temporal's enforcement. refusal() runs as the update's validator: a customer closing their own case, a second close, or a close after the lapse is refused inside the workflow, whoever calls.
  • Temporal owned the clock. The 30-minute lapse is a timer in the workflow, cancelled here because a colleague came. Before T-028 it was a sweeper loop only the demo server ran.
  • A stale fact, found by this capture. After the hand-back, pending_escalation_id is cleared, but facts.awaiting still lists escalation:E-6C40E1D0. Harmless today; wrong in the hand-off context of any later escalation in the same conversation. Recorded as F-046.

Part 03

The agent, end to end

What it is, what it can do, what happens when a message arrives, and every piece of the code in the order a message meets them. Written on 13 September, before Keycloak, Chatwoot, Temporal, Saleor and Langfuse: where it describes identity, approvals, escalation stores or the shop, the first part is what is true now.
